sections.heading: Build understanding, not just a working screen
paragraphs: AI can turn a description into code quickly, but a convincing demo does not tell you whether the data is protected, failures are handled, or future changes will be safe. This free course helps you examine those decisions rather than leave them to a coding tool.

Andrej Karpathy popularised the term vibe coding in February 2025 for building by telling AI what you want. Here, the aim is to combine that speed with enough software knowledge to judge and maintain the result—not to promise instant engineering expertise.

sections.heading: Who should take this course
paragraphs: This course is for newcomers to software development, especially people already experimenting with AI-built applications. You do not need a computing degree; curiosity and a willingness to investigate are more useful starting points.

sections.heading: What you will learn to do
bullets: Trace a user action from the interface through server logic to stored data.
Find your way around source files, configuration, repository history and project documentation.
Explain simple design choices and their compromises.
Give AI small, well-scoped tasks whose results you can review.
Check behaviour with tests, code review and systematic debugging.
Release an application and keep it secure, usable and dependable.

sections.heading: The central principle
paragraphs: Generating code faster makes checking it more important, not less. You remain responsible for understanding whether the software does the right thing.

sections.heading: A repeatable six-step approach
bullets: Begin with a practical question: establish the problem before learning the terminology.
Unpack the idea in everyday language, using a diagram when helpful.
Locate the idea in Taskboard, the running example.
Follow a worked scenario in manageable steps.
Compare common beginner errors with mistakes AI may introduce.
Try an exercise, then check your understanding.

sections.heading: Meet Taskboard
paragraphs: Taskboard is a deliberately modest task tracker: users create accounts, add tasks, assign due dates and mark work complete. Its familiar features let us study accounts, APIs, data storage, access rules, testing and operations without an unusual product getting in the way.
We start by defining its purpose and users, then explore its internals, make design choices, implement features and prepare it for ongoing use.

sections.heading: What the callouts mean
bullets: Key idea: a principle worth pausing to remember.
In Taskboard (blue): how the topic appears in the example application.
Walkthrough (grey): a guided example with successive steps.
Common mistakes (amber): traps people frequently fall into.
When AI gets it wrong (red): unreliable generated suggestions and ways to detect them.

sections.heading: Learn with an AI assistant
bullets: Attempt exercises before asking AI to critique your reasoning.
Ask for explanations of why a choice makes sense, rather than only requesting code.
Compare answers with the lesson and actual code; investigate disagreements instead of trusting confident language.
Keep your own vocabulary list alongside each part’s glossary.

sections.heading: What to have ready
paragraphs: You should be comfortable installing applications, have tried an AI assistant, and be willing to enter explained terminal commands. Prior programming is not required: lesson 5 introduces reading code, and unfamiliar terms are explained as they arise.

Use a computer, a free editor such as VS Code, Git and an AI assistant or coding agent. The learning route does not require paid services. Exercises involving hosting, charges or real user information identify that risk and provide a free or local option.

sections.heading: Choose your project
paragraphs: You can apply the lessons to your own idea, beginning with an application brief in Part 1, or build and explore Taskboard. The complete working example, including tests and documentation, is at https://github.com/solomonpromise/taskboard and can run locally without a hosting account.

Teaching examples simplify the screens and code. For their counterparts in the full application, consult docs/book-map.md in the repository. You can implement Taskboard from the brief, design pack and lesson 25 task format, or study the existing implementation as you learn.

sections.heading: Choose a starting route
bullets: For a first prototype, focus on lessons 1–3, 5–15, 17 and 24–28. These are the essential lessons marked with a star in the roadmap.
Then cover lessons 4, 16, 18–23, 29 and 30–34 to deepen design, delivery and maintenance skills. Complete this material before releasing to real users.
Start at the beginning if the vocabulary is unfamiliar; revisit the reference appendices whenever a command or file type interrupts your progress.

sections.heading: Working safely and working alone
paragraphs: Warnings identify exercises that touch external services, money or real data. Choose the local alternative when you do not need those risks. Where a workflow normally involves another reviewer or an approval, use the suggested self-review approach; a team is not a prerequisite.

sections.heading: Part 1: Understand software applications
paragraphs: Lessons 1–4 explore software categories, user problems, requirements and the development lifecycle.
Practical outcome: Define who the application serves and produce an application brief.

sections.heading: Part 2: Understand how applications work
paragraphs: Lessons 5–12 connect programming, interfaces, backend logic, HTTP, APIs, databases, data models and account permissions.
Practical outcome: Trace an action through your application and draw how its pieces communicate.

sections.heading: Part 3: Understand the project
paragraphs: Lessons 13–18 cover folders, repositories, Git collaboration, environments, dependencies, secrets and documentation.
Practical outcome: Set up a project, explain its organisation and make a controlled change.

sections.heading: Part 4: Make design and architecture decisions
paragraphs: Lessons 19–23 turn requirements into boundaries, technology choices, data and integration designs, and quality trade-offs.
Practical outcome: Create a design pack that explains the structure and the reasons behind it.

sections.heading: Part 5: Build with AI
paragraphs: Lessons 24–29 cover coding tools, task preparation, incremental implementation, generated-code review, testing and debugging.
Practical outcome: Deliver and verify the first genuinely useful version.

sections.heading: Part 6: Ship and maintain software
paragraphs: Lessons 30–34 address hosting, releases, production visibility, recovery, data protection and ongoing change.
Practical outcome: Deploy the application and write a practical maintenance guide.

sections.heading: Consolidate each stage
paragraphs: Each part closes with a project, a glossary and answers for checking your work. The appendices provide quick references, reusable planning formats, review lists and directions for further learning.

sections.heading: Keep private and generated files out
paragraphs: The commit guidance describes ordinary application repositories. Do not commit actual credentials or private user data. Ignoring a file does not remove an already tracked copy or erase it from history.

sections.heading: Stop and assess the risk
bullets: rm -rf can delete directory trees without prompting.
sudo runs with elevated privileges.
curl … | sh executes downloaded code.
git push --force can overwrite shared history.
git reset --hard discards working changes.
Any production database command deserves an explicit impact check, backup and recovery plan.

appendices.title: HTTP, API and SQL reference
appendices.intro: Quick reminders for reading requests, interpreting responses and working with relational data.

rows: Retrieve a representation; should not alter application data.
Yes, for a correctly implemented endpoint.
Create a resource or request an action.
Only with supported deduplication, such as an idempotency key.
Replace the state of a resource.
Normally yes: repeating the same request has the same intended effect.
Depends: setting a value and incrementing a value behave differently.
Normally yes in effect, although later responses may differ.
No Content: success without a response body.
Moved Permanently: use the new location.
Not Modified: a conditional read can reuse its cached representation.
Bad Request: the request is invalid.
Unauthorized: valid authentication is missing or required.
Forbidden: access is refused, often because permissions are insufficient.
Not Found: no visible matching resource; may conceal a resource from an unauthorised caller.
Conflict: the request conflicts with the current resource state.
Unprocessable Content: the request format is understood but its instructions cannot be processed.
Too Many Requests: the client has exceeded a rate limit.
Internal Server Error: the server encountered an unexpected failure.
Bad Gateway: an upstream response was invalid.
Service Unavailable: the service cannot handle the request at present.

sections.heading: SQL examples
paragraphs: These examples use PostgreSQL-style placeholders and syntax. The example schema has tasks, labels and task_labels tables.

rows: SELECT id, title FROM tasks WHERE owner_id = $1 ORDER BY due_date NULLS LAST LIMIT 50;
INSERT INTO tasks (owner_id, title, due_date) VALUES ($1, $2, $3) RETURNING id;
UPDATE tasks SET is_done = true WHERE id = $1 AND owner_id = $2;
DELETE FROM tasks WHERE id = $1 AND owner_id = $2;
SELECT t.title, l.name FROM tasks t JOIN task_labels tl ON tl.task_id = t.id JOIN labels l ON l.id = tl.label_id WHERE t.owner_id = $1;
CREATE INDEX tasks_owner_idx ON tasks (owner_id, is_done, due_date);

sections.heading: Parameters and ownership
paragraphs: Bind $1, $2 and other parameter values through the database driver rather than inserting input into SQL strings. Obtain the owner identity from the authenticated session, and scope user-data operations to that owner. Parameter binding prevents values being interpreted as SQL; it does not replace permission checks.

appendices.title: Review, release and maintenance checklists
appendices.intro: Use these lists to make checks repeatable, while adapting them to the risks of your application.

sections.heading: Review a change — lesson 27
bullets: Every edited file belongs to the agreed task; unrelated changes have been removed.
Acceptance checks cover empty input, invalid input, duplicates and attempts to access another user’s data.
User-data queries enforce ownership, bind input parameters and avoid one database query per list item.
Credentials stay out of source; the server validates input; logs and browser responses do not leak sensitive information.
Failures are handled or reported rather than silently ignored.
Added dependencies exist, are trustworthy and maintained, and solve a real need.
New configuration is supplied through the environment and documented safely in .env.example.
The implementation respects existing module boundaries and conventions instead of duplicating helpers.
Tests exercise the agreed behaviour, the full suite passes and affected documentation is current.

sections.heading: Prepare a release — lesson 31
bullets: Automated pipeline checks succeed and the change is small enough to review properly.
Database changes remain compatible with the running application and a recent production backup exists.
Migrations have been tried in staging against representative data.
Quick post-release checks are ready and the rollback procedure has been exercised.
Monitoring and alerts are active, and the release is recorded.

rows: Sort new issues, errors and user feedback; assess dependency-update pull requests.
Practise restoring data; review spending and capacity; reduce some technical debt; verify documentation and AGENTS.md still match reality.
Check architecture decision review triggers, rotate long-lived credentials and audit access permissions.

appendices.title: Further study
appendices.intro: Once the foundations feel familiar, choose a deeper topic that solves a problem you are actually facing.
